questions.q: What does Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending do?
options: Reorders the process objects by CPU, highest first, without removing or changing any of them
Deletes every process using less than average CPU
Converts the objects to plain text sorted alphabetically
Filters out all processes except the one using the most CPU
questions.explain: Sort-Object only reorders objects by the named property; -Descending reverses the default ascending order.

questions.q: When sorting by more than one property, such as Sort-Object -Property StartTime, CPU -Descending, how does PowerShell use the second property?
options: It sorts by the first property first, and only uses the second property to break ties within each group of the first
It ignores the first property entirely and sorts only by the second
It averages the two properties into a single sort value
Multi-property sorting is not supported in PowerShell
questions.explain: Order matters in a multi-property sort: the first property takes priority, the second breaks ties.

questions.q: In the worked example finding the top 5 SQL Server processes by memory, what does @{Name="MemoryMB";Expression={...}} do inside Select-Object?
options: Creates a calculated property — a custom column computed from an expression
Deletes the WorkingSet property from the object
Renames the entire Get-Process cmdlet
Sorts the results by memory automatically
questions.explain: A calculated property lets Select-Object add a custom column, here converting WorkingSet bytes into a rounded megabyte value.

questions.q: In a pipeline that filters, sorts, and selects, why does the order of those stages matter?
options: Each stage only receives what the previous stage passed through, so filtering before sorting changes what gets sorted versus sorting a smaller, already-filtered set
PowerShell ignores stage order and evaluates all stages simultaneously
Order never matters — the three cmdlets always produce identical output regardless of sequence
Select-Object must always be the very first stage in any pipeline
questions.explain: Since each pipeline stage passes its output to the next, filtering, sorting, and shaping in a different order changes what reaches each subsequent stage.

questions.q: What does Chapter 3 add, according to this lesson's chapter close?
options: Saving commands into a real .ps1 script file, plus if/else, loops, and functions so a script can make decisions
A repeat of Chapter 2's pipeline content with no new material
Exclusively cloud-based Azure PowerShell content
This lesson closes the entire course, with no further chapters
questions.explain: Chapter 3, Scripts & Control Flow, moves from interactive pipelines into saved .ps1 scripts with control-flow logic.
